name: Hookline Independent Freight Hauler Street Kit
description: An independent freight hauler's kit — not corporate-issued, assembled piece by piece from what works. The outermost layer is a faded charcoal-brown canvas work jacket, well past its original color, with a hand-applied Hookline patch on the back — a fish hook through a circuit board, the unofficial emblem of GLMZ's independent hauler collective. Pockets are everywhere: two chest, two hip, two internal, and a long vertical map pocket on the left inner lining. The collar has been modified with a strip of orange retroreflective tape added by the wearer, a common self-modification among non-affiliated haulers who need hi-vis compliance without corporate markings. Beneath the jacket is a dark green thermal henley, thick-seamed and pill-resistant, tucked into wide-leg cargo trousers in a dark slate synth-canvas with reinforced seat panels, a gusseted crotch, and a full-circumference adjustable waistband with a removable belt that holds two tool loops and a snap-clip ring. The cuffs of the trousers are tucked into mid-calf lace-up boots in worn brown synthetic leather with steel toe caps and oil-resistant soles. A knit wool-blend beanie in dark olive, often pulled back to expose the neural port behind the left ear, completes the look. Everything fits like it's been worn in over years.
functionality: High pocket count for independent hauler tool and document storage, removable belt with tool loops and snap-clip ring, neural port clearance via beanie positioning, retrofitted hi-vis compliance tape, oil-resistant steel-toe footwear, gusseted trousers for full range of motion in loading and climbing contexts.
what_it_says: You work for yourself and that means you work twice as hard for half the guarantee. The Hookline patch isn't a brand — it's a signal to other independents that you're not Stratum, not Sable Freight, not anyone's property. You've got your own route and your own contacts and you'd like to keep both. Scrappy. Self-sufficient. Quietly networked.
worn_by: circuit-tier gig workers moving cargo off the books
manufacturer: Self-assembled; jacket from Slagside surplus, trousers from Ironpass off-cuts, boots from Morrow & Sons, Hookline patch handmade or sourced through the collective
price_range: Φ250–Φ380 (accumulated over time; not purchased as a set)
story_hooks: The Hookline patch on a hauler's jacket is actually a coded signal — the specific placement and thread color indicate what cargo the wearer is currently moving and whether they're available for a side contract.
An independent hauler in this kit knows every unofficial loading bay and back-channel entry point in a district the players need to access quietly — but they want something moved in return.
A hauler has gone missing on a routine run. Their kit has shown up in a pawn market on Circuit level — everything intact, neural port access beanie still folded inside the jacket pocket.
related_entities: TESSERA CORPONATION Aegis CorpSec Hardened Security BCI

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian street hauler's silhouette—blocky and functional, layered for durability and weather. The overall impression is weathered independence: a person built for cargo runs and ungoverned zones, not corporate logistics. The faded jacket dominates, sitting loose over a compact frame, with visible hardware and patches telling a story of self-assembly and street collective pride.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and purposeful—nothing tailored. The jacket hangs slightly oversized for layering and movement; cargo trousers are wide-legged with a reinforced seat and crotch gusset for climbing and crouching. Boots are sturdy and grounded. Everything sized for functionality over aesthetics, worn-in soft at the seams.
physical_description.primary_material: Canvas work jacket (faded, weathered); dark green thermal henley (thick-seamed synthetic blend); slate synth-canvas cargo trousers (reinforced panels); brown synthetic leather boots (oil-resistant); dark olive wool-blend beanie.
physical_description.texture: Rough, lived-in, broken-in. Canvas is soft and frayed at edges; thermal henley shows pilling from years of wear; trousers have a slightly stiff weave with visible stitching; boots are scuffed and creased from use; beanie is loose-knit and supple.
physical_description.color_scheme: Muted earth tones: faded charcoal-brown jacket, dark green henley, slate-gray trousers, worn brown boots, olive beanie. Orange retroreflective tape strip on collar is the only bright accent—functional hi-vis, not decorative.
physical_description.closures: Jacket: worn button-front with some buttons replaced or missing. Trousers: full-circumference adjustable waistband with snap closures, removable belt with friction-fit. Boots: traditional lace-up with metal eyelets, knotted tight. Beanie: pull-on, no closure.
distinctive_features: Hand-applied Hookline patch on back: fish hook through circuit board, collective emblem
Orange retroreflective tape strip on collar, self-modified for hi-vis compliance
Extensive pocketing: two chest, two hip, two internal, long vertical map pocket on left lining
Tool loops on belt and snap-clip ring for carabiners/gear
Reinforced seat panels and gusseted crotch on trousers
Steel toe caps on boots, oil-resistant soles
Visible wear: fraying seams, faded patches, creases at joints, scuff marks on boots
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4–5 working class/sub-grade. No corporate insignia, fully self-assembled from surplus and off-cuts. The Hookline patch signals collective membership over corporate affiliation.
physical_description.cultural_context: Independent freight hauler, GLMZ collective member, ungoverned zones operative. Wearing this signals distrust of corporate logistics, street credibility, and self-sufficiency. The neural port visible at the nape (when beanie is pulled back) suggests light augmentation—typical for independent haulers navigating unregulated cargo routes.
physical_description.condition_typical: Weathered and broken-in, not pristine. Seams show fraying, colors are faded, boots are scuffed and creased, fabric shows minor stains and wear patterns consistent with years of active use. Patches may be hand-stitched or glued; some buttons may be mismatched replacements.
